the_day: Claude users can now turn Artifacts into desktop apps, Meta launched its Muse agent in the UK, OpenAI published protein-design research, a new Gemini setting separates chat history from AI training, and xAI had no new announcements.

items.headline: Claude users can turn Artifacts into Mac and Windows desktop apps
points: Claude Artifacts can now be turned into standalone desktop apps for macOS and Windows, The Decoder reports.
Unite.AI and Superpower Daily say users can install custom tools built with Claude as desktop apps.
9to5Mac describes it as a new way for Claude users to make Mac apps.
items.for_you: If you build tools in Claude Artifacts, you can now run them as their own apps on Mac or Windows.

items.headline: Gemini setting separates chat history from AI training
points: Gemini users can now keep their chat history while turning off use of their chats for AI training, 9to5Google reports.
Bitdefender reports that Google still keeps Gemini chats for two months even when history is turned off.
items.for_you: If you use the Gemini app, you can now keep your chat history and still opt out of AI training.

items.headline: Meta's Muse personal AI agent launches in the UK
points: Muse, Meta's personal AI agent, is now available to adults in the UK.
Meta says users can connect it to their apps for jobs like chasing a refund or renewing car insurance.
Retail partners include Sainsbury's, Argos, M&S and ASOS; the Evening Standard reports UK regulators issued warnings after the deals.
items.for_you: If you are an adult in the UK, you can now use Muse and connect it to your apps to handle tasks for you.

items.headline: OpenAI says GPT-6 models designed proteins that bound lab targets
points: OpenAI published research saying GPT-6 models designed protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code.
OpenAI says lab tests found evidence of binding across five targets.
Superpower Daily and The Defiant say the designs came from GPT-6.2.

items.headline: Engineer accused of bugging OpenAI released on $1 million bond
points: A judge ordered the release on $1 million bond of Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi engineer accused of secretly recording meetings at OpenAI.
Tom's Hardware and Gizmodo report that filings say he had hundreds of recordings, including discussions of possible trade secrets.
Engadget and Tom's Hardware report allegations that he was affiliated with, or in frequent contact with, the Saudi government.
